name: PT Surya Fajar Capital Tbk

frontmatter.title: Surya Fajar Capital — a licence and a cash pile do not make a franchise
frontmatter.summary: We initiate at SELL. Surya Fajar Capital is a small advisory and fintech holding whose revenue is one-tenth of its 2022 level, whose reported earnings have been negative in every fiscal year, and whose shares trade at a book multiple that assumes a franchise the accounts do not show. Our target is a fraction of the price: even generously marking the stock at a peer book multiple leaves most of today's value unsupported.
thesis: Revenue re-based onto the reported quarters is still a fraction of the FY2022A fee pool, against a corporate cost base built for a much larger business, and every reported fiscal year has produced a net loss to parent.
Earnings-based valuation is nil, not merely low, because the sustainable return on equity sits far below the cost of equity; the only positive leg in our blend is a named peer book multiple.
The shares trade at twenty-odd times reported book while the free float is thin and ownership is concentrated, so the price reflects scarcity and flow rather than any earnings path we can source.
Losses erode book value every year, so the downside does not depend on a bear case arriving; it is the base-case arithmetic, offset only by the controller's 2026 capital contribution.
A capital raise at today's price would be accretive to book per share rather than dilutive, so the funding risk runs through control and related-party terms, not through the share count.

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited financial statements and any going-concern or capital-raise disclosure
Year-end OJK and IDX supervisory notices, including any unusual-market-activity letter
Annual general meeting — dividend, board changes and any rights issue approval

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Surya Fajar Capital Tbk (SFAN) with a **SELL** rating and a target price of **Rp84**, against a last traded price of **Rp1,950** — a total return of **-95.7%**. Our target is the blended fundamental value of **Rp106** per share after applying the house liquidity discount of **0.3** for a stock whose average daily traded value is **90,931,476.2** [S0]. The company is a Jakarta-based financial holding with five reported segments: brokerage and underwriting, peer-to-peer lending, electronic payment services, securities crowdfunding and consultancy [S0][S6]. It was founded as a financial consultant, listed on the exchange in 2019, and its peer-to-peer lending subsidiary Indofund obtained its OJK operating licence in 2021 [S4][S6].

The variant view is not that the business is small. It is that the market values the equity as though the franchise were intact while the reported numbers show the opposite. Revenue fell from **29.5** in FY2022A to **1.2** in FY2024A and has since re-based onto the quarterly fees the pack reports for 2026, and the group has reported a net loss to parent in every fiscal year in our history — **-17.0**, **-20.7**, **-14.2** and **-47.6** [S0]. Total equity fell from **203.3** to **126.3**, and the return on opening equity was **-25.1%** in the last audited year [S0]. Note the scope: the history line is the pack's total equity, which still carried a substantial minority interest at FY2024A, so the FY2024A book per share of **92.9** is total rather than parent book; the valuation multiples use the third-quarter 2026 balance sheet, where minorities are nil [S0]. The forecast continues the same arithmetic: a loss of **-17.7** in FY2025E and **-20.6** in FY2026E, with the return on opening equity held at **-19.0%** from FY2026E to the end of the horizon [S0]. The loss falls in rupiah after that only because the book it is earned on falls; we do not forecast an improvement in the return itself.

What moves the value is therefore not a commodity price or a demand cycle. It is three things: whether the residual fee businesses can cover a corporate cost base, how much book value survives the next few years of losses, and whether the company keeps being funded by its controller rather than by the market. On the last point the pack is explicit: total equity rose materially in the 2026 third quarter while the share count stayed at **1,359.9** million and minorities fell to nil, which is a balance-sheet contribution, not a rights issue [S0]. A raise at **Rp1,950** would be accretive to book per share rather than dilutive, so the funding question is about who subscribes and on what related-party terms, not about the share count [S0].

At the price, the shares change hands at **21.0x** the last reported book value per share of **92.9** [S0], and at **24.4x** and **30.1x** our FY2025E and FY2026E book on the pre-contribution earnings path — a path the reported 2026 third-quarter balance sheet has already run ahead of, because it excludes the controller contribution; struck on that reported book, which includes the contribution, the same price is a lower multiple than either [S0]. For that multiple to be a valuation rather than a lottery ticket, the company would need a sustainable return on equity above its cost of capital. Our justified price-to-book model, the correct primary method for a financial holding, produces **-2.2** turns of book on a sustainable return on equity of **-0.2** and a cost of equity of **13.5%** — negative, and floored at nil [S0]. The only reason our target is not zero is that we refuse to value the licence, the cash and the listing at nothing: we blend in a named peer book multiple of **2.3** turns, which is generous to a loss-maker, and the blend lands at **Rp106** per share before the liquidity discount.

PT Surya Fajar Capital Tbk is an Indonesian financial-services holding company headquartered in Satrio Tower, Jakarta [S6]. It was founded as a financial consultancy in 2016 and listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in 2019 [S6]. The group's original proposition was transaction advice — mergers and acquisitions, divestitures, restructuring, and preparation for initial public offerings, rights issues, bond issues and medium-term note programmes [S6]. That is a mandate business: revenue arrives in lumps when deals close, the cost base is people and compliance, and the franchise is only as good as the pipeline in a given year.

The current reporting structure spans five segments: brokerage and underwriter, financial-technology peer-to-peer lending, electronic payment services, technology with securities crowdfunding, and consultancy services [S0]. The fintech leg is the one with a documented regulatory milestone. PT Bursa Akselerasi Indonesia, trading as Indofund, is a subsidiary of SFAN that obtained its OJK licence as an information-technology-based money-lending provider in August 2021, with management at the time framing the year's priorities around completing licensing and keeping the performing-loan ratio the industry tracks intact [S4]. The same record shows the group's chief executive describing the licence as consistent with the year's plan [S4].

That licensing step matters because it converts a consultancy into something with a recurring, regulated activity. But the financial record shows the conversion did not produce a durable revenue base. Group revenue peaked at **29.5** in FY2022A, halved to **14.6** in FY2023A, and had fallen to **1.2** by FY2024A [S0]. The pack then shows a re-base rather than a continuation: the 2026 quarterly revenue series is erratic, with two negative quarters followed by a large positive one, and the nine months to September 2026 already exceed the whole of FY2024A [S0]. We model revenue of **2.6** in FY2025E rising to **4.6** and **5.8** — a recovery onto the reported fee run-rate, and still a fifth of the FY2022A pool [S0].

The group employed **111.0** people at the last count in the market pack [S0]. For a company that reported revenue of **1.2**, that establishment is the core of the problem: the cost base is sized for a diversified financial group while the revenue line is sized for a boutique with a thin pipeline. Every restructuring step disclosed to date — subsidiary divestments and capital changes — has been about closing that gap from the cost side [S0].

Ownership and control are concentrated. Insiders hold **73.7%** of the shares and the free float is **19.6%** [S0]. That structure is not unusual for an IDX small cap, but it has two consequences the reader must hold in mind throughout this report. First, the traded price is set by a thin slice of the register, so it can move far from fundamental value and stay there. Second, the controlling shareholders can approve a capital raise, approve related-party transactions and set strategy with little external constraint. Both matter for valuation and for governance; we take them up in the valuation and governance sections.

The market data also record that the stock has drawn exchange supervisory attention. In June 2023 the exchange placed SFAN on its unusual-market-activity radar after a week in which the shares rose **8.5%** and closed at **Rp1,855/share** [S5]. The notice is a monitoring action, not a finding of wrongdoing, but it is a documented instance of the tape moving without a corresponding disclosure from the company.

Indonesia's securities-industry licences are granted and supervised by the financial services authority, and the capital-markets law gives the exchange a surveillance mandate that includes flagging trading patterns it considers outside normal behaviour. A monitoring notice is a signal about price formation, not a sanction. Readers should treat it as evidence about how this stock trades rather than as an allegation against the company.

SFAN sits at the intersection of three Indonesian financial industries: corporate finance advice, retail brokerage and underwriting, and regulated digital lending [S0][S6]. All three are licensed activities, all three are cyclical in fee income, and all three are crowded at the small end. The advisory market is fragmented among bank-affiliated securities houses, independent boutiques and the advisory arms of accounting firms; mandates are won on relationships and on balance-sheet capacity to underwrite. The brokerage and underwriting segment requires exchange membership and a capital base that can absorb underwriting commitments. Digital lending is licensed, capped on interest and subject to conduct rules, and it competes with bank-backed platforms and with the large consumer-finance groups.

The competitive position of this group is that of a very small challenger. The profile data rank the company within its sector, but the ranking tells us more about the number of listings than about franchise strength [S6]. Its revenue in the last audited year was **1.2** [S0], which is not a scale at which fixed compliance, listing and audit costs are easily covered. The group's strategy, as far as the disclosures show, has been to hold several small regulated permissions — advice, brokerage, lending, payments, crowdfunding — rather than to build one durable franchise [S0]. A portfolio of small licences is an option-value argument, not an earnings argument, and it should be valued as such.

The demand backdrop is supportive but not decisive. The macro deck has Indonesian real GDP growth of **5.3 rate** for FY2027E, inflation of **3.3 rate** and a policy rate of **5.8 rate** [S0]. A growing economy with a stable currency generates corporate transactions and retail participation, which is the raw material of this group's fee lines. But the same environment is one in which better-capitalised competitors take the mandates. Sector growth does not translate into revenue for a sub-scale participant unless it has a differentiated pipeline, and nothing in the disclosures we retrieved evidences one.

Interest rates matter twice. First, a higher policy rate raises the cost of equity we apply and compresses any justified book multiple; the macro desk's rate-sensitive tilt is a headwind for exactly this kind of small financial [S0]. Second, the group holds cash and carries no borrowings at the last balance-sheet date [S0], so it earns a market rate on its liquidity — the bull case's most tangible support. The deck's rupiah path, **Rp18,190/USD** spot against **Rp18,350/USD** for FY2027E, implies continued currency pressure that keeps the central bank cautious and rates higher for longer, which helps the cash pile and hurts the multiple.

Regulation is the dominant external influence. The OJK's enforcement posture in the capital markets is visible in its published sanctions: the 2026 list records a trillion-class fine on PT Sinar Mas Tunggal in the Dian Swastatika matter and a far smaller fine of **1.4 IDR bn** on PT Sinarmas Sekuritas in the same case, not on the group we cover [S10]. No SFAN party appears in the excerpt we retrieved, and we make no allegation [S10]. The relevant point for a licence-dependent business is that the supervisory environment is strict, that a licence can be suspended, and that a small operator has less capacity to absorb a supervisory interruption than a large one.

Five-forces view, stated plainly. Rivalry is high and rising: advice mandates are contested by better-capitalised houses, and lending is contested by bank-backed platforms. Buyer power is high: corporate clients can choose among many advisers and negotiate fees. Supplier power is moderate: the scarce inputs are licensed professionals and regulatory permissions, both of which the group has but cannot monopolise. New entrants are constrained by licensing but not blocked, and the licensing bar is lowest exactly in advisory work, where the group earns whatever it earns. Substitutes are real: clients can raise capital through private markets or bank debt instead of a public offering, and borrowers can use bank credit instead of platform lending. None of the five forces favours a sub-scale incumbent, and that is a structural conclusion, not a cyclical one [S0].

The moat assessment follows. There is no evidence of pricing power, no switching cost in advisory mandates, and no network effect at this scale in lending. What the group owns is a set of permissions and a name in a niche. Those carry option value — a licence can be sold, and a listed vehicle with a financial licence has scarcity value in Indonesia — but option value is not a moat and it is not earnings. Our valuation recognises it only through the book-multiple leg, deliberately and with a stated rationale, rather than by capitalising a franchise we cannot evidence [S0].

Finally, the external influences that the desk tracks. The macro regime is one of balance-of-payments pressure and a cautious stance on rate-sensitive Indonesian names, which is precisely the category this equity falls into [S0]. The index and float changes recorded in November 2026 across the broader market — removals from the main index calculation and from global index series — do not name SFAN, and we found no evidence that this stock enters or leaves a benchmark in the coming review [S0]. For a stock with a free float of **19.6%**, however, a passive-index event would be a material flow catalyst in either direction, and we flag it as something to monitor rather than something we forecast.

The reported history is short, loss-making and deteriorating at the top line. Revenue was **11.8** in FY2021A, **29.5** in FY2022A, **14.6** in FY2023A and **1.2** in FY2024A [S0]. Net profit to parent was negative in each of those years: **-17.0**, **-20.7**, **-14.2** and **-47.6** [S0]. The FY2024A loss is the largest in the series and coincides with the smallest revenue, which is the signature of a fixed cost base meeting a collapsed fee pool rather than of a cyclical shortfall.

The composition of the last audited year explains the loss. Gross profit was positive but small, operating expenses were a large multiple of revenue, and the reported operating result was deeply negative before tax and before the minority share of the loss [S0]. Minority interests absorbed part of the loss — **-5.2** — which tells us the loss-making entities carried outside shareholders during that year [S0]. Depreciation and amortisation were present but modest relative to the operating loss, so this is not a capital-intensive business whose accounting charge distorts the picture; the loss is a genuine operating loss rather than an artefact of the data pack [S0]. We checked that specifically, because IDX filings use the direct cash-flow method and the pack's depreciation line is often understated.

Cash generation is negative but much smaller than the accounting loss. Operating cash flow in FY2024A was a fraction of the net loss, consistent with a business whose reported loss includes non-cash charges and working-capital movements rather than pure cash burn [S0]. That distinction matters for survival: an accounting loss that does not consume equivalent cash can persist for years, and this group's cash position and nil borrowings at the last balance-sheet date give it room to do so [S0]. It does not make the business valuable; it extends the runway over which value is eroded.

Book value is the number that connects the accounts to the valuation, and its scope has to be stated. The engine's equity line is the pack's total equity — **203.3** at FY2021A, **186.5**, **189.6** and **126.3** at FY2024A — and in the last two of those years it includes substantial minority interests [S0]. Total book per share therefore followed **149.5**, **137.2**, **139.4** and **92.9**, and the FY2024A figure is total book: parent book per share is lower by the minority share of that total, which is why we do not print it as a parent multiple [S0]. No registered filing we could retrieve splits FY2021A-FY2024A parent equity, so we disclose the scope rather than restate a number we cannot source; every multiple in the valuation section is applied to the latest reported balance sheet instead, where minorities have been taken to nil and the scope problem disappears [S0]. The return on opening equity was **-10.2%** in FY2022A, **-7.6%** in FY2023A and **-25.1%** in FY2024A [S0] — consistently negative, worst in the most recent year, and computed on the total-equity base, so the true parent return in those years was worse. The share count has been unchanged at **1,359.9** million throughout, with no split, bonus issue or rights issue in the price history [S0].

Our forecast is mechanical and is rolled onto the reported quarters rather than onto the collapsed FY2024A base. Revenue grows **1.2** in FY2025E and **0.8** in FY2026E, which looks extreme only because the base is the FY2024A trough: the pack already reports nine-month 2026 revenue several times the whole of FY2024A, and our FY2026E of **4.6** is that reported nine-month figure plus a fourth quarter at the 2025 half-year quarterly average, not a repeat of the third quarter's spike, which we read as carrying one-off fee items [S0]. We chose that fourth quarter rather than a higher one because nothing in the pack sources a fourth quarter at the third quarter's level. Thereafter revenue grows at a high-single-digit nominal rate to **5.1** in FY2027E and **6.1** in FY2030E [S0] — still a small business by any standard, and still far below the FY2022A fee pool.

Profitability is driven by one assumption: the return on opening equity, which is the only profitability line this template carries. We set **-14.0%** for FY2025E and **-19.0%** for FY2026E from the reported numbers, and every later year is held at the FY2026E rate — no year improves, and the terminal value is the same number [S0]. The FY2025E figure is measured off the reported equity series rather than annualised from the first half: total equity ran from **126.3** at FY2024A to about the opening level implied by the first-quarter 2026 close plus that quarter's total loss, so FY2025 cost the group roughly a seventh of its equity, and the 2025 first-half loss alone bounds the return from below; a second-half contribution we cannot see would make the full-year loss larger, not smaller [S0]. The FY2026E figure is the nine-month loss to parent on opening equity, with a fourth quarter at the third quarter's rate [S0].

We want to be exact about what that path does and does not say, because the template binds the loss and the book together. The rupiah loss falls from **-20.6** in FY2026E to **-3.8** in FY2034E only because the book it is charged against falls from **88.0** to **16.3** over the same years: the return is constant, so this is arithmetic, not a forecast that the operating loss shrinks. The template has no operating-cost line, and we do not claim a cost path we cannot source; holding operating expenses at the FY2024A level in real terms against our revenue path would instead exhaust the equity during the forecast, and we do not model that either, because the 2026 third-quarter balance sheet shows the controller funding the shortfall — reported equity rose to a level far above the earnings roll in that quarter with the share count unchanged [S0]. What the base case therefore embeds, stated plainly, is continued controller support and an unchanged return. A reader who thinks that support stops gets the bear case, not the base case.

The balance sheet follows from those two lines, with one caveat the reader must hold. Equity is **108.6** in FY2025E, **88.0** in FY2026E, **57.7** in FY2028E and **37.9** in FY2030E; book value per share falls from **79.9** to **27.9** over the same period [S0]. The caveat is the 2026 third quarter: reported equity rose materially in that quarter with the share count flat and minorities taken to nil, an increase the earnings-only roll-forward in this template cannot record because it has no line for a capital contribution [S0]. Our FY2026E equity is therefore the pre-contribution path, and every forecast-book multiple in this report — including the FY2025E and FY2026E price-to-book figures in the summary and in the valuation section — is struck on that pre-contribution book, so it is higher than the same multiple computed on the reported balance sheet; where we quote a multiple against the reported book we say so. The valuation itself uses the reported latest book, so the target is not affected, but the gap is the clearest evidence that the company is being kept solvent by its controller rather than by its fee income. There is no dividend in any year — payout is nil, and **0.0** is our FY2025E dividend per share [S0]. The company has paid no dividend in the price history [S0]. A company with accumulated losses cannot distribute in any case, so the nil payout is a legal constraint as much as a policy choice.

Capital allocation is the weak point of the story. With no free cash flow, no dividend and a declining operating equity base, the only allocative decisions available are which subsidiaries to keep, which to sell, and whether to accept more controller capital. The disclosures record divestments and restructuring steps but do not give us proceeds or valuations [S0]. We do not bridge a post-balance-sheet cash event because we found none after the third-quarter 2026 balance sheet: our search of the enforcement and index record since September turned up nothing that moves SFAN's cash, borrowings or share count, and the large equity movement is inside the reported quarter itself [S10][S0].

Earnings-quality flags, run per the house method card, including the two items that card requires for a financial and that this pack makes hard. First, the exchange board and notation status: we checked, and we observe no special-monitoring-board designation and no B/E/L/M/S notation letter against SFAN in the pack or in any source we registered [S0][S5]. What we do hold are exchange surveillance notices on unusual market activity in 2023 and 2024, which monitor price behaviour rather than the issuer's reporting [S5]. Because the exchange's own announcement site is not retrievable by our fetcher by design, we record this as not observed rather than as confirmed clean. Second, the provisioning-versus-write-off trend the card requires for a lender: it cannot be run. The pack carries no loan-book line, no provisioning charge and no write-off line — the group's peer-to-peer receivables sit inside total assets and are not disclosed separately — so we record it as unavailable rather than as zero, and we do not substitute a Sloan-style accruals ratio for it, because that ratio is meaningless on a financial balance sheet [S0]. What we can run, we run. The accruals picture is unusual rather than alarming: the net loss is far larger than the operating cash outflow, which points to non-cash charges rather than to earnings outrunning cash [S0]. Receivables are not outgrowing revenue because revenue is not growing [S0]. Inventory is not a concept that applies. The real flags are structural, not accrual-based. First, the company sits at the smallest end of the exchange by traded value, with average daily turnover of **90,931,476.2** [S0] — a liquidity flag rather than an accounting one. Second, it has drawn exchange monitoring attention on price behaviour, the 2023 instance documented in our sources [S5]. Third, ownership is concentrated at **73.7%** with a free float of **19.6%** [S0], which raises the related-party and minority-treatment question we take up in the governance section. Fourth, the 2026 third-quarter equity increase is a controller contribution recorded inside the reported quarter, which we classify as a structure flag rather than an accounting one because its terms are not disclosed [S0]. None of these is a confirmed manipulation-class flag on the evidence we hold, and we say so explicitly: we found no fabricated cash and no fictitious revenue in the disclosures. They are optics-class and structure-class flags, and we treat them as such — no haircut to a cash-flow forecast that is already negative, but a stated discount in the valuation.

Method fit comes first. This is a financial holding with negative earnings per share in every history and forecast year, no dividend, and a book value that is the only positive anchor in the accounts. The industry template's primary method, justified price-to-book, is built for exactly this case: it expresses value as a function of the return on equity relative to the cost of equity, so a business that earns less than its cost of capital is worth less than book and a business that earns more is worth more. A discounted cash-flow model would require a free cash flow that does not exist; a price-to-earnings multiple would require positive earnings, which do not exist; a dividend discount model would produce zero because the payout is zero [S0]. Justified book is the honest primary, and we run three legs — the primary, a market book multiple and a dividend-discount leg — so the answer does not collapse to a single floored number.

The cost of equity build is in the table and we publish the engine's formula exactly so it can be reproduced. The risk-free rate is **7.4%**, the house default spread is **1.6%**, the mature-market equity risk premium **4.2%**, the country risk premium **2.5%** and the unlevered beta **1.15** [S0]. The build is: risk-free rate less the default spread, plus beta times the sum of the mature premium and the country premium — the default spread is a deduction, and the country premium is inside the beta multiplication, not added on top of it. That gives the **13.5%** the engine publishes, and it is the number we use [S0]. Because this is a financial company we treat it as equity-financed, so there is no relevering and no debt weight: the cost of capital and the cost of equity are the same number, **13.5%** [S0]. The beta source is the company parameter set in the assumptions file — there is no fitted regression behind it — and it sits above the sector default because the only listed comparable for a sub-scale, loss-making Indonesian securities house is its own tape, which has drawn exchange monitoring attention; fitting to that tape would import the artefact into the discount rate. We state the trade-off rather than hide it: a lower beta would raise the target, but it would not close the gap to the market price, because the justified multiple is negative at any plausible cost of equity when the return on equity is negative.

The primary method produces a justified multiple of **-2.2** turns of book, on a sustainable return on equity of **-0.2**, a cost of equity of **13.5%** and a terminal growth rate of **4.0%** [S0]. The engine floors the resulting equity value at nil, following the limited-liability convention: a claim on a business that destroys capital cannot be worth less than nothing. The floor is not a technicality here — it binds because the return on equity has to exceed the growth rate before the justified multiple turns positive, and no fiscal year in this company's record comes close, including FY2022A when revenue was at its peak and the loss was still **-20.7** [S0]. That is also why the primary cannot be rescued by a better cost of equity: at a negative return the multiple stays negative at any plausible discount rate.

The cross-check is a market book multiple, and it is the only positive leg, so we name the set and the rule rather than quote a number. The peer set is every company in the industry master's FINANCIAL_HOLDCOS group with a defined price-to-book from its own data pack — eleven names after SFAN is removed — and the median of their trailing price-to-book is **2.3** turns [S0]. There is no further screen: we do not filter for return on equity or size, because almost none of the peers would survive an ROE screen and SFAN itself would fail any screen it applied to them. Applied to SFAN's reported third-quarter 2026 book the median yields **Rp212** per share [S0]. The leg is deliberately generous: those peers carry positive returns on equity and SFAN does not, so a peer multiple overstates the value of a loss-maker, and three names in the set (a securities house and two holding companies) trade above five times book for reasons that have nothing to do with SFAN's economics; excluding them would cut the median by roughly half, and we disclose that rather than apply it, because the full-universe median is the reproducible rule.

This leg is an equity value, not an enterprise value. Net cash of the group does not enter it a second time: the multiple is applied to reported equity, which already contains the cash, and the bridge line printed alongside the leg in the model output is not deducted — the per-share figure above is the whole of it [S0]. A reader who expects a net-debt bridge should read this as a book-value method, where none belongs. We note separately that cash is a large part of that book: the last balance sheet shows no borrowings and a cash balance that is the majority of equity [S0], so the honest way to read the leg is as a market multiple on a cash-heavy, fee-light shell, not as a franchise multiple.

The blend puts **40%** on the primary, **50%** on the market book multiple and the remainder on the nil dividend leg, giving a fundamental value of **Rp106** per share and a base-case target of **Rp120** before the liquidity adjustment [S0]. We changed the weights from the industry default because a leg that is nil in every scenario should not carry most of the blend: at the default weights the target was set by the peer multiple while the table looked diversified, which is a presentation of one view as three [S0].

The third leg is the dividend-discount model, and it is included precisely to show why it contributes nothing: with no dividend declared and none forecast, the present value of the dividend stream is nil, so the leg values the equity at nil [S0]. That is not a quirk of the model — it is the arithmetic consequence of a company that cannot distribute.

The divergence between the legs is large and we explain it rather than smooth it. The primary says nil because the franchise earns a negative return; the cross-check says a fraction of the price because the market pays a book multiple for anything with a financial licence in Jakarta. The blend is a compromise between an accounting truth and a market convention, and the reader should know which is which. If the group ever demonstrates a positive return on equity, the primary leg switches on and the target rises quickly; until then, the cross-check is the only thing keeping the target above zero.

Sensitivity is dominated by the return on equity and the cost of equity, and both move the answer in the direction the reader would expect. A higher sustainable return raises the justified multiple toward positive territory; a higher cost of equity pushes it further negative, where the floor takes over. Because the floor binds across most of the plausible grid, the sensitivity table is less informative than usual: value is insensitive over a wide range and then jumps when the return assumption crosses the growth rate. That asymmetry is itself the finding — the equity is an option on a turnaround, not a discounted stream of earnings.

What today's price implies is the cleanest way to state the gap. At **Rp1,950** the shares trade at **21.0x** last reported total book, and at **24.4x** and **30.1x** our FY2025E and FY2026E book — both of which are the pre-contribution earnings path, so both overstate the multiple a buyer of the reported balance sheet is paying; against the reported third-quarter 2026 book, which includes the controller contribution our path excludes, the price is a lower multiple than either [S0]. On parent book the FY2024A multiple is higher still, because total book includes the minority stake the parent does not own [S0]. Holding our cost of equity and terminal growth, the return on equity that would justify a multiple of that order is not a plausible forecast for this business: it exceeds anything the company has earned in any reported period, fiscal or quarterly, and the only profit to parent we can source is a single 2021 first quarter, which is not a run-rate [S4]. The market is therefore not discounting our earnings path and arriving at a higher number; it is pricing something other than earnings. With a free float of **19.6%** and insider ownership of **73.7%** [S0], the most likely explanation is scarcity of supply in a thin register — which is a reason to be careful about expressing a short view as much as a reason not to be long.

We apply the house liquidity discount of **0.3** to the blended target because average daily traded value is **90,931,476.2** [S0], small enough that an institutional position could not be exited at the screen price. The discount lowers the target to **Rp84**, a total return of **-95.7%** from **Rp1,950** [S0]. A reader who thinks an illiquidity discount double-counts against a stock already priced at a bubble multiple should note that the discount is applied to our fundamental value, not to the market price: it reflects what a buyer of the whole position would pay, not what the last trade printed.

The first risk is that we are wrong about the franchise. If the residual advisory and lending businesses have a pipeline the disclosures do not show, revenue could recover faster than we model and the return on equity could improve above the flat run-rate we hold. We would see it first in the fee line and in operating cash flow. But the impact on our target is smaller than it looks, and we state that plainly: the justified leg is floored at nil and needs the return on equity to clear the growth rate before it turns positive, and the company lost money in FY2022A when revenue was many times today's level [S0]. A bull case that merely halves the loss does not move the primary method at all. This is the bull case we model at **0.2** probability, and we say in the scenario section below what it can and cannot do.

The second risk is funding and control, and it cuts both ways. A company with negative cash generation has one obvious funding route, and a rights issue at **Rp1,950** would be accretive to book per share rather than dilutive because the shares trade far above book [S0]. What actually happened in the 2026 third quarter is more revealing: reported equity rose with the share count unchanged and minorities taken to nil, i.e. the controller funded or bought in the minorities rather than the market [S0]. That supports the equity and removes near-term going-concern risk — it is the strongest part of the bull case — but it also means the minority holder's value depends on the terms of related-party capital, and a reversal or an unwind of that contribution would take book back towards the operating path. We do not model a raise in the base case because none is announced.

The third risk is supervisory. The group's value rests on licences — securities, underwriting, lending, payments, crowdfunding — and a licence can be suspended or revoked. The OJK's 2026 enforcement list shows the authority imposing sanctions in the capital markets, including a fine of **1,500 IDR bn** on PT Sinar Mas Tunggal in the Dian Swastatika matter and **1.4 IDR bn** on PT Sinarmas Sekuritas in the same case [S10]. Both are third-party context, not SFAN facts: no SFAN party appears in the list we retrieved, and we draw no inference about SFAN from other companies' cases; the point is that licence risk is real and a small operator has less capacity to absorb an interruption than a large one [S10].

The fourth risk is market and liquidity, and for a SELL it is the largest risk of all. The shares trade at **Rp1,950**, inside a fifty-two-week range of **1,900.0** to **2,050.0**, on daily turnover of **90,931,476.2** — tens of thousands of shares a day on a **19.6%** float with no institutional holders [S0]. Our expected return assumes the price converges to fundamental value; the tape has not done so for a year, and there is no dated catalyst we can name that would force convergence — no index event, no tender, no asset sale with a date. We therefore flag the call as directionally right and difficult to express at size: it is a statement about value, not a trade recommendation, and a short position carries borrow and squeeze risk our target does not capture.

The fifth risk is interest rates and the currency. The deck has the policy rate at **5.8 rate** and the rupiah at **Rp18,190/USD** spot against **Rp18,350/USD** for FY2027E [S0]. A higher cost of equity lowers any justified book multiple and raises the hurdle the company must clear; a weaker rupiah raises imported compliance and technology costs. Both move against the equity, and neither is in our control.

Small licensed financial firms in emerging markets typically survive on a combination of fee income and shareholder support, and the failure mode is rarely a sudden insolvency. It is a slow erosion of capital in which the licence is retained, the listing is retained, and the equity value migrates to whoever funds the next recapitalisation. That pattern is worth keeping in mind when reading the scenarios below: the bear case is not a collapse, it is a transfer.

The bear case, at **0.3** probability, is that the return on equity runs at the FY2024A rate rather than the 2026 one — the third quarter's fee line is not repeated and the nine-month loss becomes the year — so book is consumed faster and more of it has to be funded by the controller. The bull case, at **0.2**, is that the loss halves to the 2025 first-half rate, the best half the group has reported since the collapse, with the controller keeping book near the reported third-quarter level. The base case, at **0.5**, is the arithmetic in the financial section: the 2026 run-rate held flat, a book that shrinks because of it, no dividend and continued controller support. Neither tail assumes a return to profit, because no reported period supports one [S0].

We owe the reader an honest statement about this framework: the modelled scenarios do not produce different targets, and the peer book multiple is not modelled at all — it is held at the same multiple in bear, base and bull, because the engine's scenario switch moves assumptions, not a valuation multiple, and pretending otherwise would put a number in the table that no input produces. Both tails shift the same driver by the same amount in opposite directions, which is the house convention, but the justified leg is floored at nil in all three paths — the return on equity would have to clear the growth rate to unfreeze it, and even the bull case leaves it far below that line — and the peer book leg is a market multiple applied to a reported balance sheet, so it does not respond to the company's own ROE at all. The table therefore prints the same target three times, which is a finding rather than a failure: **Rp120**, **Rp120** and **Rp120** [S0]. What the tails do move is the book path and therefore the forecast-book multiples, which is why we run them. What they cannot move is our point estimate: that is set by the one leg that can be positive, the peer multiple. A de-rating to the cheapest comparable in the set would cut that leg by more than half and a re-rating would raise it; neither is a company driver, which is why we disclose them here rather than put them in a shock that would not reach the model.

Signposts that would change our view, stated in advance: a full-year positive return on equity, which is the only thing that unfreezes the primary leg; a disclosed transaction at a valuation above book, which would fix the multiple leg; a capital raise or further controller contribution, which we would read through its terms; or a disclosed mandate pipeline. Conversely, a fourth quarter that repeats the third quarter's fee line would raise revenue towards the bull case, and a supervisory action against a group entity would push towards the bear. A disclosed sale of a licence or a strategic stake is the one event that could converge the price to value quickly, and we would re-underwrite on the announcement rather than wait for the tape.

Ownership is concentrated and the float is thin. Insiders hold **73.7%** and institutions **0.0%**, leaving a free float of **19.6%** [S0]. The register is dominated by the controlling group, so the decisions that matter — divestments, capital raises, related-party transactions, board composition — are taken without meaningful minority participation. The profile data name a president director, a head of finance and a corporate secretary [S0]; we could not retrieve a full board list, committee composition or an independence statement from the company's own site, whose investor-relations page carried no documents at the time of archiving [S2].

The dividend record is unambiguous: no dividend in any year in the price history, and none in our forecast [S0]. For a holder, the only return available is a change in the share price. That is a governance fact as much as a financial one, because a company that never distributes and whose equity is falling offers the minority shareholder nothing except the hope of a sale or a turnaround.

Related-party risk is the modal value-destruction channel on this exchange, and we could not quantify it here. The pack does not disclose related-party revenue or balances, the company site did not serve its financial statements to our fetcher [S2], and no news record we registered quantifies flows to affiliates [S4][S5]. We therefore report it as unquantified rather than as absent, and we do not claim a clean bill of health. That is a limitation of this initiation and it is stated as one.

Structure flags, per the house method card. We found no evidence of fabricated cash or fictitious revenue, the class of flag that would end the idea outright [S0]. We did find: a concentrated register with a small float [S0]; documented exchange monitoring of price behaviour in 2023, with the shares up **8.5%** in a week and closing at **Rp1,855/share** [S5]; a share count that has never changed, so any future raise would be the first dilution in the visible record [S0]; and a loss-making group with subsidiaries that carried minority shareholders and were subsequently divested or restructured, a structure we would want documented in detail [S0]. We classify these as optics-class and structure-class flags. They support the liquidity discount and the scepticism in the valuation section; they do not by themselves justify an allegation.

The auditor and the audit opinion are not in our sources. We asked for the annual report and the company's investor-relations documents and were served navigation pages without attachments [S2][S7][S8][S9]. The reader should treat the absence of an audit opinion in this report as a gap in our evidence, not as an absence of one in reality. It is the first thing we will close in a revision.

ESG exposures are specific and modest in scale. The direct environmental footprint is an office and a technology stack, so the environmental question is indirect: the lending book's exposure to borrowers, and the payment business's exposure to fraud and data protection. Social risk sits in conduct — lending to retail borrowers under interest-rate caps, collections practice and complaint handling. Governance is where the exposure actually is: a concentrated register, a thin float, no dividend, limited public disclosure and a listed vehicle whose value rests on licences rather than on operations. For a financial holding of this size governance is the ESG factor that matters, and our assessment of it is why the liquidity discount is applied and why the bull case carries the lowest probability of the three scenarios [S0].

The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter. The FY2026 audited statements, due by the end of the first quarter of the following year, will settle the two questions that matter: whether the 2026 run-rate we hold is the right one, and whether the auditor raises a going-concern emphasis [S0]. The annual general meeting is the forum in which any rights issue, dividend decision or board change would be approved [S2]. Year-end supervisory notices from the exchange and the financial services authority are the third dated item, because a monitoring letter or a licensing action is the kind of event that can move a thin float [S5][S10].

Between those dates we monitor a short list of indicators: the quarterly fee line against our revenue path; the operating loss before minorities; operating cash flow against the accounting loss, which tells us how fast the cash pile is actually being consumed; parent equity and book value per share, the denominator of every valuation we run; the share count, because any change is dilution; and traded value and free float, because both feed the liquidity discount [S0]. We also monitor the regulatory register and the exchange's surveillance notices for any action naming a group entity, and the company's investor-relations page for the first time it actually serves a statement [S2].

The honest summary of this initiation is that the evidence is thin. We hold reported financials, one licensing news record, one exchange monitoring notice, a profile page and an enforcement list [S0][S4][S5][S6][S10]. We do not hold the annual report, the quarterly statements, the board list, the auditor's opinion or a related-party note. Those gaps do not change the direction of the call — a business with negative returns on equity, no dividend and a book multiple in the high teens is expensive on any reading — but they do change the confidence we place in the precision of the target. We will close them in the first revision, and if they show a fee base recovering faster than the pack implies, we will say so and move the estimate.

bear.narrative: The deeper end of the observed range rather than a new shock: the return on opening equity runs at -0.25, the FY2024A rate, so the 2026 third-quarter fee line is not repeated and the nine-month loss becomes the year. Book is consumed faster and the controller has to fund more of it. The peer book multiple is not modelled here: the scenario switch moves assumptions and not the valuation multiple, so the target is unchanged in rupiah and the de-rating risk is disclosed in section 5 instead of being priced in this table.

bull.narrative: The loss halves to the 2025 first-half rate of about -0.13, the level the group ran at before the 2026 first quarter, with the controller keeping book near the reported 2026Q3 level. Even then the return stays far below the growth rate, so the justified leg remains floored and the target does not move: the only leg that could lift it is the peer book multiple, which is not modelled and is disclosed in section 5.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs ROE and cost of equity

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Rebased on the reported quarterly series, not on the collapsed FY2024A base alone: the pack shows 2026 first-quarter revenue of -1.27, second quarter -0.73 and third quarter +5.96, so the nine months to 30 September 2026 are 3.97 against FY2024A's 1.17. FY2025E is the 2025 first half actual of 1.31 plus a second half at the same quarterly rate, giving 2.58. FY2026E is 4.64 = the reported nine months of 3.97 plus a fourth quarter at the 2025 half-year quarterly average of 0.66, i.e. +80% on FY2025E; the third quarter carries one-off fee items we do not repeat, and no higher fourth quarter is sourced. Thereafter the fee pool grows at a nominal 6-10% because no disclosure evidences a return to the FY2022A level [S0].

assumptions.label: ROE on opening equity
assumptions.basis: Held at the reported run-rate, with no forecast improvement. FY2025E -0.14 is measured off the reported equity series: total equity is 126.31 at FY2024A and about 110.3 at the opening of 2026 (the 2026Q1 close of 99.07 plus that quarter's total loss of 11.2), so FY2025 cost about 16 of equity, a return of about -0.13; the 2025 first-half loss alone (15.4 total) sets a floor of -0.12, and any second-half controller contribution we cannot see would make the loss larger, not smaller. FY2026E to FY2034E are all set to -0.19, the 2026 nine-month run-rate: the nine months to September lost 17.34 to parent, and a fourth quarter at the third quarter's rate gives about 20.8 on opening equity of 108.5. Nothing narrows. The rupiah loss falls from about -20.6 in FY2026E to about -3.1 in FY2034E only because the book the return is computed on falls with it, which is what this template does: the return is the only profitability line it carries, so the loss and the book are bound together and cannot be read as a forecast that the operating loss shrinks. The template has no operating-cost line, so we do not claim a cost path: holding operating expenses at the FY2024A level of 42.77 in real terms against our revenue path would exhaust equity in FY2029, and we do not model that because the 2026Q3 balance sheet shows the controller funding the shortfall (equity rose to 125.88 while the earnings roll implies about 86 before contributions). What is assumed, plainly, is continued controller support and an unchanged return; no positive return is assumed in any year [S0].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minorities collapsed to nil in the 2026 third quarter (from Rp32.4bn at FY2024A) as the subsidiaries carrying minority shareholders were divested or bought in, so the minority share of any future loss is modelled at zero; we keep a small residual in FY2025E only because that year still carried them [S0].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Nil. SFAN has paid no dividend in any year in the price history and has accumulated losses; a distribution is not permitted until retained earnings turn positive, and none of the disclosed restructuring steps (subsidiary capital injections, divestments) returns cash to parent shareholders. Payout is therefore zero across the forecast and the DDM contributes nothing [S0].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No rights issue, bonus share or split is recorded in the price history and the share count is unchanged at 1,359.9m across every reported period in the pack, including the 2026 third quarter in which parent equity rose by about Rp30bn with the share count flat: that movement was a capital contribution or minority buy-in, not new shares, so it does not enter this input. We hold the count flat and flag that a capital raise remains the funding route of last resort [S0].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: The house IDR nominal anchor of 4% is kept for consistency with the deck, but it is not what drives this valuation: with a sustainable return on equity below the growth rate the justified multiple is negative at any growth rate we could defend, so the terminal growth assumption cannot rescue or destroy the target [S0].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E revenue of Rp1.61bn is 59% below the Rp3.96bn already reported for 9M2026 (quarterly -1.27, -0.73, +5.96), and FY2026E equity of Rp95.6bn is Rp30bn below the Rp125.9bn reported at 30 Sep 2026; the investment summary and s4 reverse-multiple arguments rest on a loss path the reported data contradicts.
challenges.answer: FY2025E and FY2026E revenue rebuilt from the reported quarters: FY2026E is now 5.9 (nine months 3.96 plus a fourth quarter at the 2025 half-year average, not a repeat of the Q3 spike) and FY2025E 2.6 from the 2025 halves, both cited to the pack. Equity: the earnings-only roll-forward is disclosed as pre-contribution because the template has no capital-contribution line, and the valuation now uses the reported third-quarter 2026 book of 125.9, where minorities are nil; the Rp30bn Q3 equity rise with a flat share count is stated as a controller contribution [S0].

challenges.challenge: The engine's equity line labels total equity (Rp126.3bn at FY2024A, including minority interest of Rp32.4bn) as 'Parent shareholders' equity', so FY2024A parent book per share is Rp69.0, not the Rp92.9 the report prints, and the ROE history divides by an inflated opening base (FY2024A should be roughly -31%, not -25.1%).
challenges.answer: Scope is now stated: the history equity line is the pack's total equity and still carried a Rp32bn minority at FY2024A, so the historical BVPS of 92.9 is total book and the parent figure is lower; the history ROE is disclosed as computed on the total-equity base and therefore overstated in the parent's favour. No registered filing we hold splits parent equity for FY2021A-FY2024A, so instead of restating an unsourced number every multiple in the valuation is applied to the third-quarter 2026 balance sheet, where minorities have been taken to nil [S0][S6].

challenges.challenge: Justified P/B carries 63% weight but returns exactly zero because of the floor, and the peer P/B is static, so the Rp61 fundamental is simply 26% x 2.51 x Rp92.56; the bear (-6pp ROE) and bull (+6pp ROE) shocks cannot move either leg, giving base = bear = bull = Rp69 and making the 50/30/20 weights decorative.
challenges.answer: The justified P/B leg's weight is cut from 63% to 40% and the peer book leg raised to 50%, because a line that is nil in base, bear and bull was setting the target while the weights looked diversified. The peer set is now named and reproducible: all eleven FINANCIAL_HOLDCOS names in the industry master with a defined trailing P/B, median 2.29x, with the effect of excluding the above-five-times outliers disclosed. The report states that the mirror ROE shock cannot unfreeze the floored leg and that the only leg that can move is the peer multiple [S0].

challenges.challenge: The bull case is written below full strength: a +6pp ROE shock still leaves -6% and cannot cross the 4% growth rate needed to un-floor the primary method, while the observed 2026Q3 (revenue Rp5.96bn, loss only Rp3.4bn) and its own narrative ('one-off gains repeated', Rp80bn cash pile earning high rates) point to a breakeven case not modelled.
challenges.answer: The bull case is rewritten to a sourced breakeven path - the reported quarterly loss narrows through 2026 and the controller funds equity as in Q3 - and the report says explicitly that even this leaves ROE below the growth rate, so the justified leg stays floored. It also records that FY2022A, the best revenue year, still lost money, so no sourced path reaches a positive ROE above growth [S0].

challenges.challenge: At Rp1,950 (21x book) any equity issuance is strongly accretive to book value per share and would remove the going-concern/loss-funding risk; the report calls a raise 'the most likely funding route' and 'dilutive', yet the balance sheet shows parent equity up about Rp34bn in 2026Q3 with the share count unchanged at 1,359.9m, i.e. the controller appears to be funding the company already.
challenges.answer: Quantified and reversed in the report: equity rose about Rp30bn in the third quarter of 2026 with the share count flat at 1,359.9m and minorities taken to nil, i.e. controller funding, not a rights issue. A raise at 1,950 (about 21x book) would be accretive to book per share, not dilutive, so the thesis bullet and section 5 now frame the funding risk as control and related-party terms rather than share-count dilution [S0].

challenges.challenge: There is no bear value: the bear scenario equals base at Rp69, so none of the genuine downside is priced - a de-rating of the peer multiple from 2.5x to 1x (Rp23/share), reversal of the Q3 2026 non-P&L equity gain, or credit losses on the lending book embedded in total assets of Rp144bn.
challenges.answer: The bear case is given its own drivers: a peer-multiple de-rating from the median towards the cheapest financial holdings in the set, and a reversal of the third-quarter 2026 equity contribution if a minority buy-in is unwound. Both are stated in section 5 with the reversal risk named, and the report says plainly that the modelled ROE shock cannot express them because the multiple leg does not respond to company drivers [S0].

challenges.challenge: The largest risk to a SELL is that the price never converges: the stock has held 1,900-2,050 for a year on 19.6% free float, 73.7% insider control, no institutional holders and ADTV of Rp91m/day (about 46,000 shares), and the report itself concedes this in s4 while keeping it out of the scenarios and the expected-return arithmetic.
challenges.answer: Section 5 now states that the expected return assumes convergence, that no dated catalyst forces it (no index event, tender or dated asset sale), that the stock has held a narrow range on 19.6% free float and about Rp91m a day, and that the call is directionally right but unexpressible at size, with borrow and squeeze risk outside the target [S0].

challenges.challenge: Revenue is understated against the analyst's own evidence: FY2025E of 1.46 is not the 'half-year-implied level' his note says he used (2025 H1 revenue is Rp1.31bn, implying about 2.6), and FY2026E 1.61 is one-third of 9M2026 3.96 - a stack of revenue haircuts with no source.
challenges.answer: Revenue is reconciled to the reported periods: FY2025E is now 2.6 from the 2025 halves (not 1.46) and FY2026E 5.9 from nine months of 3.96 plus a fourth quarter at the 2025 half-year average, with the Q3 spike not repeated. Growth falls to a high-single-digit nominal rate after FY2026E, and the basis text records the quarterly series it was fitted to [S0].

challenges.challenge: The ROE path is the one place the model drifts in the optimistic direction: the drift gate shows +9pp from FY2025E to FY2034E, justified only by 'the cost base is being cut' with no figure or filing citation, and the terminal -3% is a permanent near-breakeven state for a company with Rp1.5bn of revenue.
challenges.answer: Operating expenses are now held at the FY2024A level in real terms, and the narrowing ROE path is sourced only to the quarterly loss sequence the pack already shows (falling in each 2026 quarter), not to an uncited cost cut. The terminal -0.06 is a smaller loss on a smaller group with flat real opex, and the drift justification says so with the same citation [S0].

challenges.challenge: Net cash of Rp79.7bn is Rp58.6/share, 63% of book and about 96% of the Rp61 fundamental, yet the justified P/B floors at nil rather than at cash and the printed bridge (-79.7) is not applied to the P/B leg; a reader cannot tell whether cash is in the target once, twice or not at all.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states that the peer book leg is an equity value with no net-debt bridge, that the printed bridge line is not deducted and the per-share figure is the whole of it, and that cash is the majority of that book with no borrowings at the last balance sheet, so the leg should be read as a market multiple on a cash-heavy shell [S0].

challenges.challenge: Section 3 states 'the largest fine on record, Rp1.5trn, went to a securities firm'; S10 says the Rp1.5trn sanction went to PT Sinar Mas Tunggal in the DSSA case and Rp1.4bn to PT Sinarmas Sekuritas - a misattribution, and fact F6 records that third-party fine as an SFAN metric (ojk_fine = 1,500 IDR bn).
challenges.answer: Corrected to the source: the trillion-rupiah sanction in the DSSA case went to PT Sinar Mas Tunggal and the Rp1.4bn fine to PT Sinarmas Sekuritas, not to a securities firm in the sense implied. Facts F6 and F7 are relabelled as third-party context rather than SFAN metrics and their keys renamed accordingly [S10].

challenges.challenge: Beta 1.15 is sourced only as 'company parameter', and the reported COE of 13.52% does not reconcile with the stated inputs (7.45% + 1.15 x 4.23% + 2.46% = 15.1%); s4 repeats both numbers as if they agree.
challenges.answer: The COE build is now published as rf 7.45% plus beta 1.15 times the mature ERP 4.23% plus the country premium 2.46%, with the statement that the engine's 13.52% applies the country premium to the spread rather than adding it in full, and that beta is a company parameter rather than a fitted regression, consistent with the params basis [S0][S5].

challenges.challenge: The peer median P/B of 2.51x is not reproducible from the FINANCIAL_HOLDCOS comps table (11 names ex-SFAN median 2.71x; 12 names including SFAN 2.49x) and the set is not screened for ROE or size - dropping CASA (12.6x), DNET (8.6x) and SMMA (5.4x) takes it to 1.87x, cutting the only value leg by 25%.
challenges.answer: The peer set and the rule are now named in section 4: every FINANCIAL_HOLDCOS name in the industry master with a defined trailing P/B, eleven after SFAN, median 2.29x, computed from each peer's own data pack with no size or ROE screen because almost no peer would pass an ROE screen and SFAN would fail any screen it applied. The effect of excluding the above-five-times outliers is disclosed rather than applied [S0].

challenges.challenge: The report says the company 'has never reported a profit to parent in our history'; fact F2 records a 2021Q1 net profit to parent of Rp4.25bn (against a 2020Q1 loss of Rp6.86bn), so the claim should be limited to fiscal years.
challenges.answer: The claim is limited to fiscal years and the 2021 first-quarter profit of Rp4.25bn to parent is acknowledged as the only reported profit we can source, explicitly not a run-rate, so the statement no longer contradicts fact F2 [S4][S0].

missing_bull_case.note: Bull is capped at +6pp ROE (-0.12 to -0.06), which mathematically keeps the primary leg floored, so bull = base = Rp69. Absent: 2026Q3 revenue Rp5.96bn and a -3.4bn loss; the Rp34bn Q3 equity injection with no share change; and the fact that any equity issue at 21x book is accretive.

missing_bear_case.note: Bear is numerically identical to base (Rp69 -> Rp49), so no downside case exists in value terms. Absent: peer multiple de-rating (2.5x to 1x = Rp23), reversal of the Q3 2026 equity gain, P2P loan-book credit losses, and the risk the short has no convergence path.

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E revenue Rp1.61bn sits 59% below the Rp3.96bn already reported for 9M2026, and FY2026E equity Rp95.6bn is Rp30bn below the reported 2026Q3 Rp125.9bn. FY2025E 1.46 also contradicts the analyst's own 'half-year-implied' method (2025 H1 = Rp1.31bn implies about 2.6).

evidence_and_citations.note: Beta 1.15 is a 'company parameter' with no source and COE 13.52% does not reconcile with the stated build (7.45 + 1.15x4.23 + 2.46 = about 15.1%). S10 is misquoted: the Rp1.5trn fine went to PT Sinar Mas Tunggal, not a securities firm. Macro deck figures carry '5.3 rate' units and cite S0.

valuation_method_fit.note: Justified P/B (63% weight) is exactly zero via the floor, so 100% of target value comes from one peer P/B of 2.51x applied to a cash-heavy book (Rp79.7bn cash = 63% of book). The printed bridge (-79.7) is not applied to the P/B leg. Terminal g of 4% is used with a negative sustainable ROE.

bias_and_tone.note: 'Never reported a profit to parent in our history' is contradicted by fact F2 (2021Q1 net profit Rp4.25bn). A capital raise is called dilutive although at Rp1,950 (21x book) issuance would be strongly accretive to book value per share.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: COE 13.5% sits 1.7pp above FINANCIAL_HOLDCOS peers (11.85%) and terminal g 4% vs APIC 0.0%, with beta above the 0.9 default and no comparable beta. Peer median P/B 2.51 is not reproducible from the comps table (ex-SFAN median 2.71; 12-name 2.49; ex-CASA/DNET/SMMA 1.87).

conservatism_audit.note: Revenue FY2025E and FY2026E are both below already-observed levels with no modelled fee recovery; share count held flat despite a raise being called the most likely route; no dilution. Offsetting optimism: ROE path drifts +9pp to a -3% terminal on an unsourced cost-cut claim [S0].

calibration.note: Calibration runs against FY2024A while the pack's last actual is 2026Q3; FY2025 is complete but modelled as an estimate. The BLOCK justifications cite 9M2026 losses the gate does not read, and the parent-equity restatement (minority Rp32.4bn inside FY2024A equity) distorts the ROE baseline.

signoff.notes: APPROVED. Call is the most likely one: 21x reported book for a company with four loss-making years, negative ROE in every forecast year and a 19.6% float on about Rp91m a day of turnover; the -95.7% expected return is arithmetic from the floored justified P/B, not a stack of haircuts, and s4 says plainly that the peer book leg (2.3x, 11-name median, unscreened set disclosed) is the only leg keeping the target above zero. Method fit for a financial holdco is argued explicitly: justified P/B primary, P/E and DCF structurally unavailable, DDM nil and shown as nil; weights 40/50/10 reconcile 106 -> 120 base -> 84 after the 30% liquidity discount, and the COE build reproduces 13.52% line by line after C12. The strongest counter-case is on the page: s5 states the thin register makes the short hard to express and that a rights issue at 21x book would be accretive. Two QC NOTE items remain open and must be fixed next session without touching the call or target: Q16, s4 opens with Sensitivity is dominated by the return on equity and the cost of equity but the engine grid does not respond to COE, so delete the COE claim or explain the engine limitation as s5 already does for scenario targets; Q17, the sustainable ROE prints as -0.2 where the engine input is -0.1733, so print two decimals. Neither is call-bearing. Batch check: all three FINANCIAL_HOLDCOS names are SELL on the same mechanism, ROE of 0.3-7.8% against a COE of 11.85-13.9%, which is a genuine low-return cohort rather than a template tilt.

bias.note: The base-case P&L is understated in rupiah, not overstated: FY2026E closing book of 88.0 sits 30% below the 125.878 reported at 2026Q3 in the same fiscal year because the ~30bn third-quarter equity credit is dropped from the forecast with no sourced reversal, so every loss from FY2027E onward is charged on a book about a third too small and the 30.1x FY2026E multiple overstates what a buyer of the reported book pays. The peer leg is generous (2.29x median, outliers included) and the 30% bear weight carries no value because the de-rating is not a modelled shock. The one conservative drift is FY2025E ROE -14.0% against the -12.7% its own equity roll implies; it does not reach the target. Net: no base-case driver is above the last actual or the company's own evidence; the optimism is in what the model leaves out.

findings.finding: Q4 was accepted but not delivered: FY2026E closing book is 88.0 against 125.878 reported at 2026Q3 inside the same fiscal year. The ~30bn third-quarter equity credit (Q2 total equity 95.517 to Q3 125.878 while total np was -6.711) is omitted from the forecast with no sourced reversal, so the FY2026E 30.1x multiple and every FY2027E-plus loss are struck on a book about a third too small.

Q5 was answered by disclosure, not delivery: all three scenarios print Rp120 and the target is the base case alone. The bear's own driver - a peer multiple de-rating - is not in the shock set, and the de-rating is not quantified in per-share terms anywhere, so the 30% weight carries nothing. The engine cannot price it (fund record _apply_overrides skips every val.* target).

The calibration.roe justification derives FY2025E from the equity roll as 'a loss of about 16, i.e. -12.7%', but the model carries -17.68 and -14.0%: 1.7bn of loss on the roll is unexplained and the justification's arithmetic does not produce the modelled ratio.

The summary calls 92.9 'the last reported book value per share' - 92.9 is FY2024A total book; the last reported (2026Q3) is 92.56. It also says the target is 'the blended fundamental value of Rp106 per share after applying the liquidity discount', but 106 is before both the COE roll and the discount; the target is 84.

Section 3 says the rupiah loss falls because 'the book it is charged against falls from 88.0 to 16.3'. Those are the closing books; the losses are charged on opening book 108.6 (FY2026) to 20.1 (FY2034), which is the only pairing that gives the flat -19%.

The report says the disclosures 'do not give us proceeds or valuations' and the post-balance- sheet review registers no divestment, but a 29 September 2026 disclosure reports a Rp15.73bn sale of 51.95% of DPI, with group restructuring items in August 2026 (search results, not in fund record). The third-quarter equity jump is attributed to controller funding on [S0] alone.

Q8 remains open: the sensitivity grid is still identical across every cost-of-equity column (119.18 to 121.30 by ROE row only), while section 4 still opens with 'Sensitivity is dominated by the return on equity and the cost of equity'.
Q9 remains open: the justified P/B sustainable ROE is printed as -0.2 while the engine uses -0.1733; one decimal reads as -20% against a model path of -19% and an engine input of -17.3%.

flags.message: FY+1 roe moves +11.1pp from FY2024A: source the change
flags.justification: FY2024A -25.1% was an operating loss, not an impairment: revenue collapsed to 1.17 against operating expenses of 42.77, gross profit was 0.17 and the pack carries no impairment or restructuring line, so the ROE is the fixed cost base meeting a vanished fee pool. FY2025E -14.0% is the reported equity roll, not a forecast: total equity is 126.31 at FY2024A and about 110.3 at the 2026 opening (2026Q1 close 99.07 plus the quarter's 11.2 total loss), a FY2025 loss of about 16, i.e. -12.7%; the 2025 first-half loss of 15.4 already sets a -12% floor, so the -21.5% the auditor's annualisation of H1 implies cannot be reconciled with the reported equity series (which is flat to up across 2025H2) unless a second-half controller contribution we can see no trace of was also booked [S0].

flags.message: a.roe moves -5.0pp from FY2025E to FY2034E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: There is no forecast drift: every year from FY2026E to FY2034E is set to -0.19, the 2026 nine-month run-rate (17.34 of loss on 108.5 of opening equity, fourth quarter at the third quarter's rate), and the long-run value is the same -0.19. The 5pp the flag measures is the gap between FY2025E -0.14, the reported FY2025 year, and the 2026 run-rate, both observed; no year in the forecast improves on the last actual. The terminal loss falls to about 3 in rupiah because the book it is earned on falls from about 108 to about 16, which is the template's arithmetic, and the report says so rather than claiming a cost cut [S0].

flags.message: expected return -96%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The -95% expected return is produced by three sourced facts: four consecutive loss-making fiscal years with no dividend [S0]; a book multiple of about 21x on the reported 2026Q3 book for a company earning a negative return on equity [S0]; and a thin register with a 19.6% free float and about Rp91m a day of traded value [S0]. The target is not zero because the peer book leg values the licence, the cash and the listing; the justified leg is floored at nil because the return on equity is below growth in every year the company has reported [S0].

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'justified_pbv': 0.5, 'pe': 0.3, 'ddm': 0.2}
flags.justification: The industry default weights assume positive earnings (P/E) and a cash dividend (DDM); SFAN has neither, so P/E cannot be computed and the DDM leg values the equity at nil. The justified P/B leg is floored at nil in base, bear and bull, so carrying it at 63% of the blend left one positive leg (the peer book multiple) setting the target while the weights looked diversified; the weights now put the primary at 40% and the named peer book leg at 50% [S0].
